title: Eirwen's Mud Pie Mishap
markdown:
The fair buzzed. Popped corn. A hundred conversations. Stalls along the village green offered pumpkins like grumpy orange giants and rockets that wobbled with optimism. In the middle of that cheerful clutter stood Eirwen.

Eirwen the beaver was the neatest baker the river had. She could seat a dam to the width of a whisker, but her heart lived in the kitchen. Lists: ingredients measured, steps numbered, hiccups anticipated with crisp checkmarks. You would not have found a crumb off-duty in her ordinary week.

This year the stall was Mud Pie. Not mud. Rich dark chocolate mounds, cocoa-dusted, tidy as hills on a map. Eirwen, paws precise, felt the name sit too plain on such a day. She wanted a title that turned heads and then mouths.

"Mina," she said, settling a tiny bright-blue baker's hat that threatened to leave at the next ear-twitch. She unfurled a scroll tied in red ribbon and tapped it as if it were law. "Today we unveil the Magnificent, Mystical, Mud Pie Masterpiece Experience. Each pie a portal. A culinary journey for the discerning palate."

Mina the tortoise blinked the long blink of a friend who has heard grandeur before. She ambled close, shell a familiar weather. "They look very nice, Eirwen. Little chocolate hills. Ready for climbing."

Eirwen's whiskers worked. The grandeur, she was sure, had not yet been grasped. She smoothed an already smooth apron. "Presentation. Narrative. That is how one captures the essence." The hat got a firmer shove.

The fair opened. Chatter rose. Eirwen stood behind lists spread like maps and practised a sophisticated smile in a jam-jar's shine.

"Welcome, esteemed patrons. An unparalleled confectionery revelation. Observe the artisanal precision. The structural integrity. These are not mere mud pies, but terrestrial delights of exquisite decadence."

A few people paused, puzzled in a polite way. A small child with a lollipop pointed, helpful as a bell. "She talks funny, Mummy."

Eirwen's ears dipped a fraction. The majestic aura she had booked failed to arrive. Paws that knew a dam's geometry went clumsy on a plate. She wanted, very much, to be seen as calm control in a hat.

"And here," she declared, lifting a mound dusted like velvet, "the Whispering Woods Wonder. Subtle earthy tones. Ancient forest after rain." She offered it to a passing lady. Eloquence and a slick of cocoa disagreed.

Splat.

The Wonder landed on a very important-looking gentleman's crisp white shirt. Chocolate bloomed. Silence arrived, heavier than the rides. He stared. Eirwen froze. Hazel eyes went from stain to crowd, which had begun to consider tittering. The Masterpiece Experience had found the ground.

Retreat offered itself: the lists, a polite hole in the afternoon. Then Mina's gaze, steady as a river stone. Eirwen had come to make something wonderful. Wonderful, it seemed, would have to use the shirt.

"Oh, dear." The voice that came out surprised her: booming, theatrical, a fairground of its own. "The mud pie has made its grand unannounced landing. A terrestrial delight, indeed. It appears our pies have opinions today. They are eager to share, one unexpected application at a time."

She picked up the next mound as if it were a relic and grinned, proper mischief, eyes crinkling. "This," a floury tap near, not on, the disaster, "is the Impromptu Impact Award. Surprise. Delight. Spontaneous deliciousness."

The gentleman, who had been assembling a scowl, blinked. A smile arrived late and stayed. The crowd's almost-snicker became laughter that wanted another pie.

Eirwen went in. Extra shavings, a handful. "For those who prefer artistic expression: the Abstract Aroma option." She dabbed and scattered until tidy hills became intentional messes, each one a small event. Personality, she did not announce, was doing the work the scroll had failed at.

Queues formed, not for the Masterpiece Experience, but for Impromptu Impact and Abstract Aroma. People wanted a pie that had already had an adventure. The blue hat sat jaunty. Chocolate found her paws and was not wiped off at once. The lists lay open and unread. Mina, who had never needed a portal, took a hill for climbing and did not hurry it.

Eirwen sold the next one without a speech. The gentleman, shirt famous now, bought two, which the river would later consider the neatest joke of the day.
audience: children aged 11-12, amusing story for older children
